audit.recode_to: No class change. Optional refinement of the domain note: Bowden 2001 says affixes and clitics never bear stress and 'affixation never affects stress' (§2.4 p. 53 ex. (51) ha-ˈmul, not *ˈhamul; §3.1.3 pp. 89-90; ch. 11 p. 274 demonstratives iˈne, siˈne, iˈda with unstressed prefixes), and Bowden & Hajek 1996:56 give [naˈpe] < [ˈpe]. So penultimate stress is computed on the root/stem; suffixation (-o, -ma, with unstressed-vowel deletion) keeps the penult surface-true, but prefixed or procliticised monosyllabic roots surface with word-final stress. If the catalog's domain field distinguishes word from STEM, STEM (root + suffixes, prefixes extrametrical) is the more faithful value; lexical final-stress exceptions (amseh, magun, makót; loans like aˈhad) could be noted under exceptions.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Bowden 2001 PDF we hold text at p. 51 §2.4, exactly as the locator says. Deciding source is a modern 451-page reference grammar (Pacific Linguistics 521, 2001; = 1997 PhD) with a dedicated stress section giving primary penultimate stress, secondary stress on the pre-antepenult in 4-5 syllable words, phonetic correlates, and exceptions; this is the top item in Glottolog's descriptive bibliography (all three entries are Bowden's own works) and we hold it in full. The one additional source located, the JIPA Illustration Bowden & Hajek 1996 (downloaded to, independently states the same penultimate rule (p. 56) and adds the exception classes, so it confirms the fixed-penultimate coding and the stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable) rule string. The only nuance not captured by domain=word is that stress is root/s

sources.quote: 'Stress is indicated by a greater degree of force in the production of a syllable, a noticeably higher pitch than in unstressed syllables, and some degree of lengthening. In general, primary stress falls on the only syllable of monosyllabic words or on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words. Examples of antepenultimate stress are extremely rare, e.g. [ˈttobit] "we defecate". sources.note: Only phonetician-coauthored description of Taba; independent statement of the penultimate rule plus the exception classes (rare antepenult, final stress in loans and in prefixed/procliticised monosyllabic roots) that bear on the record's domain=word field. downloaded now.
